title: Catholics disagree
hook: the Church holds deep disagreements within one communion
tomorrow: Year four close: the house of many rooms

segments.voice: Yesterday, seekers, and a pope's picture of an open courtyard for people still looking. Your line was the courtyard. When a big question came up, did you ask one more question back? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-five.

Sunday lunch after Mass. Grandpa misses the Latin. His granddaughter loves the guitar Mass. An uncle reads one Catholic newspaper, an aunt reads another, and they have opinions about each other's. Somebody says the word bishop and the table goes quiet. All of them went to the same Mass that morning. All of them received communion. All of them will be back next week. For days now we've been looking outward, at neighbors of other faiths and none. Today the neighbor is sitting across the table, in the same pew. Catholics disagree.
screen: `SUNDAY LUNCH, AND OPINIONS.` → `THE SAME MASS THAT MORNING.` → `THE NEIGHBOR IN THE SAME PEW.`

segments.voice: Start with the apostles, because they argued too. In his letter to the Galatians, Paul describes a clash with Peter at Antioch over eating with Gentile believers. Paul doesn't soften it. In the Douay-Rheims he writes: "I withstood him to the face." Two apostles, one Church, a public disagreement, and the New Testament keeps it on the record. The Catechism names where this comes from. It says that from the beginning the one Church has been marked by great diversity, because God gives many different gifts and the people receiving them are different too. Then it names what holds the diversity together: one faith professed, common worship and sacraments, and the succession of bishops from the apostles. Above all of them, it says, is charity, the bond of perfection. So the Church draws a line between two kinds of questions. Some things belong to the faith itself, and there the Church asks for unity. But other questions are left open: how to apply teaching to a hard case, which style of prayer helps, which school of theology makes the most sense. The Church's history has room for these arguments. Dominican and Jesuit theologians once argued so hard about how grace works that a pope finally let both schools keep teaching, and told them to stop calling each other heretics. An old Latin saying, which Pope John XXIII quoted, gives the shape of it: in necessary things unity, in doubtful things liberty, in all things charity. That's what one communion looks like up close. Not everyone thinking alike. Everyone at the same altar.
screen: `PAUL WITHSTOOD PETER TO HIS FACE.` · `DIVERSITY FROM THE BEGINNING.` · `ONE FAITH, ONE WORSHIP, ONE BOND OF LOVE.` · `UNITY, LIBERTY, CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to disagree kindly with someone. Settle, and breathe. Choose one person you disagree with, about church, or politics, or how to raise children, someone you'll actually see this week. Now find one thing you genuinely share with them: a person you both love, a meal you've eaten together, a Mass you've both been to. Hold that for a moment. Then choose one sentence you could say that names your view without belittling theirs. If you pray, you can ask for patience for you both. The bell holds the time.
Catholics disagree. From the apostles on, the Church has held real disagreements inside one faith, one worship and one bond of charity. Today's word.
Your line: unity, not sameness. Today, in one disagreement, say what you share before you say where you differ. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics share one profession of faith and the same sacraments while holding different views on many open questions, from theology to liturgy to politics. Parishes include people who disagree, and the Church allows different schools of theology and spirituality within its communion.

trapdoor: what you thought: being Catholic means everyone agrees on everything.
what it means: Catholics share one faith, one worship and one bond of charity, and still disagree on many open questions.

notes: Douay-Rheims Galatians 2:11: 'But when Cephas was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed.' Only 'I withstood him to the face' is quoted. Confirm. The clash is summarized as being over eating with Gentile believers (2:12); confirm.

Catechism 814–815 paraphrased: diversity from the beginning (variety of God's gifts, diversity of recipients); bonds of unity: profession of one faith, common celebration of worship, especially the sacraments, apostolic succession; above all charity, 'the bond of perfection' (Colossians 3:14). Confirm.

The controversy de auxiliis: Paul V ended the debate (1607; no date given in the voice) allowing both Dominican and Jesuit positions to be taught and forbidding them to censure each other as heretical. Confirm the summary 'let both schools keep teaching, and told them to stop calling each other heretics'.

'In necessariis unitas, in dubiis libertas, in omnibus caritas': origin disputed (often credited to Rupertus Meldenius; sometimes misattributed to Augustine); John XXIII quoted it in Ad Petri Cathedram. The voice calls it 'an old Latin saying' and gives no author. Confirm John XXIII's use.

'Other questions are left open' is a general statement; the examples (applying teaching to hard cases, styles of prayer, schools of theology) are deliberately mild. A Keeper may wish to adjust what counts as 'open'.
The hook's family lunch is illustrative; it names no specific controversy or publication.
Original: Latin, ecclesiastical pronunciation of the first phrase only.

Editor pass: varied the practice opener and close (dropped 'Bring to mind', 'See their face' and 'pray for them by name', repeated across 1422–1424); light wording change in the de auxiliis line. Facts left as written: Galatians 2:11 Douay-Rheims wording, CCC 814–815 paraphrase, John XXIII's use of the Latin saying.
